title: Earnings Are an Opinion, Cash Is a Fact

cards.headline: A profitable company can still run out of cash.
cards.body: Profit is an accounting result. Cash is a bank balance. They are not the same number, and the difference is where a lot of bad surprises live. A company can report record earnings and still miss payroll.

art.alt: Accounting profit and cash shown as two different measures rather than the same thing.

cards.headline: Revenue is booked when it is earned.
cards.body: Under accrual accounting, a sale counts the day you **ship** the product, not the day the money lands. Deliver $10m of equipment in December on 90-day terms and December's income statement shows $10m. Your bank account shows nothing until March.

art.alt: An invoice recorded now with a dotted timeline leading to cash arriving later.

cards.headline: Some costs never touch the bank.
cards.body: Depreciation spreads the cost of a machine over its useful life. This year the company charges $30m of depreciation against earnings, but **no cash moves**. The cash went out years ago, when the machine was bought.

art.alt: A long-lived asset gradually becoming an accounting expense without a new cash payment.

cards.title: From earnings to free cash flow
cards.caption: $50m of net income, plus $30m of depreciation, minus $40m tied up in unpaid invoices, gives $40m of operating cash. Capital spending takes $25m more.

cards.prompt: That $30m depreciation charge cuts reported earnings by $30m. Does it also cut this year's cash by $30m?

options.label: No, the cash left when it was bought

cards.explanation: Depreciation is a **non-cash** charge. That is why the cash flow statement adds it straight back to net income before anything else.

cards.headline: Free cash flow is what is left.
cards.body: Operating cash flow is $40m — the cash the business itself generated. But keeping the machines running costs $25m of capital spending. Free cash flow is the **$15m** that survives, and only that $15m can repay debt, buy back shares, or fund a dividend.

art.alt: Cash coming into a business minus capital spending leaves free cash flow.

cards.body: Operating cash flow was $40m. Subtract the $25m of [[1]] and $15m of free cash flow is left.
cards.explanation: Capital spending is real cash going out the door. Free cash flow is operating cash flow minus capital expenditure — the money genuinely available to owners and lenders.

cards.title: When the gap keeps widening
cards.caption: One year of earnings running ahead of cash is normal. Five years of a widening gap is a question worth asking: where is the money going?

cards.summary: Earnings are a judgment about timing. Cash flow is a record of money that actually moved.
bullets: Accrual accounting books revenue before the cash arrives.
Depreciation cuts earnings without cutting cash.
Free cash flow is operating cash flow minus capital spending.
A gap that persists for years is worth investigating.

art.alt: Operating cash after necessary investment becomes cash the owners can ultimately use.

cards.insight: Earnings tell you what a company says it made. Cash flow tells you what it actually collected. When they disagree, follow the cash.
